name: De la Finca al Mundo — COCACAP escapes the commodity trap
description: A five-round, advanced agribusiness and commodity-strategy simulation. You lead the board of Cooperativa Cafetalera y Cacaotera del Altiplano (COCACAP), a 480-family smallholder coffee and fine-flavor cacao cooperative in the western highlands of Guatemala (Huehuetenango and San Marcos, 1,400–2,000 m). COCACAP earns $1.12M a year selling commodity-grade coffee at the ICE Coffee C price plus a thin differential through intermediary exporters (coyotes) — trapped at the bottom of a value chain where the farm captures 8–18% and roasting, branding and retail capture the rest. The recently elected board has approved a five-year plan, “De la Finca al Mundo” (From the Farm to the World), to escape the commodity trap by upgrading on four fronts at once — quality, certification, market relationships and brand — while surviving the commodity price volatility that destroys unhedged cooperatives mid-transition. Over five agricultural cycles you steer a $220K Year-1 budget across wet-processing, varietal renewal, harvest quality and commodity hedging (Year 1 “El Diagnóstico”); then Q-grading, cacao fermentation, organic transition, a quality-differentiated member payment system (cuadro de calidad) and direct-trade outreach (Year 2 “La Calidad”); Rainforest Alliance and organic certification, agroforestry, EUDR plot-level traceability and a stabilization fund (Year 3 “La Certificación”); specialty-roaster and bean-to-bar partnerships, a DTC brand, export logistics and key-account capability (Year 4 “El Mercado”); and final contracts, governance and climate resilience leading into the Buyer Summit (Year 5 “La Cosecha Estratégica”). The KPIs you move are Average Cup Score (SCA, start 79.2; specialty is 80+), Premium Revenue % (start 35), Member Retention (start 87%), Price-Risk Exposure (% of next harvest unhedged), Certification Coverage, Financial Health and the live ICE Coffee C commodity price the rounds move. The math punishes the five classic errors with sticky, run-defining penalties: investing in everything in Year 1 (budget exhaustion, no crisis buffer); skipping commodity hedging (devastated by the Round-2 price collapse); pursuing certification or quality without buyer relationships — or buyers without quality (stranded certs / a failed first shipment, because capability and market must be co-sequenced); treating traceability as bureaucratic overhead (losing the biggest buyer to the EU Deforestation Regulation); and building the DTC brand before quality consistency, or paying every member the same price (free-rider quality erosion that destroys brand equity). The simulation culminates in a three-buyer Summit — Nordic Brews AB (25 MT of 85+ SCA coffee at $2.30/lb with traceability and certification), Tablón de Cacao (8 MT of fine-flavor fermented cacao at $16,000/tonne) and Cooperativa Justa (Fairtrade/Organic certified supply) — and securing all three contracts earns a 1.15× bonus. The top verdict — escaping the commodity trap — requires a clean, co-sequenced, hedged, in-budget five-year path; a blind click-through of the seeded defaults cannot win.

Cycle 1 — El Diagnóstico

Your Decisions This Cycle

Facilitator (the board, the members, and three international buyers)
Year one of “De la Finca al Mundo.” You sell clean coffee at the ICE C price plus eight cents through coyotes — the farm keeps a sliver of every dollar a roaster charges. Escaping the commodity trap means upgrading quality, certification, market and brand together, in the right order, while surviving the price collapse that is coming. Spend the whole $220K on Year-1 ambition and you'll have no buffer when it hits. Certify without buyers and the certs strand; chase buyers without quality and the first shipment fails. Build the brand on inconsistent quality and the free-rider problem will hollow it out. Sequence matters as much as ambition.
